high TPS burst handling and autoscale policies
transcript:
Header: Date: 2026-04-27 15:30 UTC, Duration: ~52m; Location: Zoom; Recording: yes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE); Marco Chen (Redwood SE); Priya Shah (Redwood PM); Carlos Rivera (Peregrine Head of ML); Meera Patel (Peregrine Platform Eng); Jordan Li (Peregrine SRE)

[00:00] Lena Ortiz: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'll keep this tight, we want to show a couple of failure modes and our playbook around them. im lena, im the ae, marco will run the deep parts.
[00:18] Carlos Rivera: thanks, lena. we care most about two things: long session context (we have clinical note histories >80k tokens in some flows) and spikes — we get occasional 3x bursts during batch imports.
[00:34] Marco Chen: got it. quick overview: Redwood handles long context via prefix KV caching + history truncation rules; for surges we have burst capacity, graceful throttles and model fallbacks. i'll demo runtime behavior and console traces.
[00:56] Meera Patel: quick question — when you say KV cache, is that per session or per model shard? we run a sharded model across 8 gpus.
[01:10] Marco Chen: per worker-host; cache entries are guid-keyed by session id. for sharded deployments we replicate minimal metadata and shard-local caches hold kv slices, so eviction is local but we coordinate via lease tokens. (slight pause) sorry that's a mouthful, but in practice you see cache hit ratios in the console metrics.
[01:34] Jordan Li: and what happens if the cache is evicted mid-stream? e.g., a session is paused and resumed after 20 minutes?
[01:46] Marco Chen: we fall back to re-populating the KV from checkpoint + we can warm the cache via prefix replay; there's a short penalty p50 jump while warmup happens. we also support a low-cost compacted prefix representation for extremely long histories to avoid O(n) prefix replays.
[02:12] Carlos Rivera: our biggest fear is request timeouts under burst. do you throttle upstream or queue requests? we have hard 30s client-side timeouts.
[02:26] Marco Chen: good question. policy choices: queueing with dynamic timeouts, shed to a lighter model, or preempt with a best-effort response (partial stream). by default Redwood offers queueing up to configured concurrency, then graceful shedding — you can configure per-route fallback to a smaller quantized model. we demo both behaviors.
[02:50] Lena Ortiz: quick note — in your contract we can set a dedicated burst pool so capacity is there, but the playbook still matters for spikes above the pool.
[03:05] Meera Patel: show us the console traces, please.
[03:12] Marco Chen: switching screens, open the console; here's a live trace from our internal stress test. you can see the timeline: p50/p95/p99 latencies, active sessions, KV hit rate. also the streaming blocks column shows bytes queued to the stream buffer.
[03:34] [screen share noises; someone mutes/unmutes]
[03:42] Marco Chen: so, here's experiment A — 1k concurrent sessions with 60k-token histories, steady state. KV hit ratio stays ~88% after warmup; p95 is ~420ms.
[03:58] Marco Chen: experiment B — short burst: 7k concurrent for 90s. console shows queue depth spike, worker GC churn, and streaming buffer grows; at ~18s you see backpressure signals and we start shedding to model-tier B (quantized) for non-critical routes.
[04:20] Meera Patel: at shed point, do you return http 429 or provide a degraded stream? we prefer degraded partial answers rather than hard errors for UX reasons.
[04:32] Marco Chen: both options. we can return a partial token stream with a 'truncated_history' flag in the response metadata so the app can decide to ask for a human review. the API will also surface a reason string (e.g., "history_truncated_for_latency"). sometimes clients prefer 429 to force retry logic.
[04:50] Jordan Li: what about client-side timeouts? if they cut at 30s, do you attempt reconnect/resume semantics?
[04:58] Marco Chen: we have session resume tokens for streaming; the server maintains a short window of KV snapshot for resume within a configured TTL (default 2 minutes but adjustable). if the client reconnects within TTL, we can resume without full replay. if beyond TTL, you'll need to replay prefix which may exceed your 30s budget. that's where compacted prefixes help.
[05:28] Carlos Rivera: can you demo that resume?
[05:33] Marco Chen: yes. i'll run a live simulated session — starting a 120k-token conversation and then cut the client at ~12s to mimic timeout, then reconnect. watch the timeline.
[05:46] [keyboard noise]
[05:58] Marco Chen: okay initiating session now — note the stream packets on the right. (short pause) cutting client... now reconnecting. you see a small spike as we rehydrate from the snapshot, then delta streaming resumes. reconnect latency ~1.1s after resume; full replay would have been ~9–10s without snapshot.
[06:26] Meera Patel: nice. do you store snapshots to disk or in-memory? we're worried about memory bloat with many snapshots.
[06:36] Marco Chen: snapshots are kept in-tiered storage: hot in RAM for recent sessions, warm on local NVMe for longer TTLs, and we have configurable TTL/capacity thresholds. when NVMe pressure rises we evict per LRU and optionally persist compact prefixes to object store.
[06:56] Priya Shah: i'd like to switch to the Optimize recommendations bit — for high tps, what are the key knobs you suggest?
[07:06] Marco Chen: Optimize recommends batching targets by request size, adjusting sequence length buckets, and quantization profiles per model. in Practice we recommend: cap long-history queries with compacted prefix for reads, enable small-batch continuous batching with 10–20ms latency padding, and setup a fallback policy to a 4-bit quant model for non-SLA routes.
[07:34] Carlos Rivera: for the medical summarization route we need deterministic outputs — quantization can change probabilities, how do you handle quality regression detection?
[07:46] Marco Chen: Redwood has eval hooks tied to your prompt sets. during pilot we run A/B on a labeled eval set and the console surfaces quality deltas. if degradation exceeds your threshold we stop rollouts automatically.
[08:02] Jordan Li: show error traces for timeout scenario, we want to see what our logs look like and how they'd map to our SRE alerts.
[08:10] Marco Chen: on the traces panel, filter by error type: here's a sample 504 (upstream timeout) and a downstream shed event with reason code "backpressure_shed"; logs include request_id, session_id, kv_hit, model_variant, and worker_id. you can hook these into your SIEM via our log forwarder.
[08:36] Meera Patel: question on security — if we use snapshotting and NVMe, do you encrypt at rest? our compliance requires envelope encryption with our KMS.
[08:46] Lena Ortiz: yes; for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM and snapshots are encrypted. for Hosted we use envelope encryption and can set customer-managed keys on enterprise plans.
[08:58] Carlos Rivera: good. now a scenario: we replay a 200k token history to a model that has a 32k context window — what happens?
[09:08] Marco Chen: two parts: history compaction and truncation. We run token-scoring to keep most informative segments, compaction reduces redundant segments into summaries, then truncate to fit the context window. you can opt to preserve the last N tokens verbatim while compacting earlier cycles.
[09:28] Carlos Rivera: does compaction risk losing critical clinical events?
[09:34] Marco Chen: it can — hence we allow rules: keep sections matching regexes, or preserve notes tagged as 'critical'. Optimize will recommend compaction thresholds based on your eval metrics so you balance cost and fidelity.
[09:50] Priya Shah: can the console simulate different policies and show expected cost impact?
[09:56] Marco Chen: yes, in the Optimize tab we have a policy simulator: pull your historical traces, let it run offline and show expected token savings, model-change risk, and projected p95 latency. i'll demo with Peregrine sample trace if you shared it — which you mentioned earlier you could.
[10:12] Carlos Rivera: we'll share a sanitized trace.
[10:16] Marco Chen: great. next, a deeper failure: sustained high TPS that induces preemption across workers causing KV eviction storms. this often looks like a cascading failure — queue depth climbs, workers OOM, new workers spin up and cause more cache warmups. our recommended playbook: 1) enable soft-queue limits with backpressure signals to clients, 2) set model-fallback stages, 3) configure warm-up pools for expected burst windows.
[10:44] Jordan Li: warm-up pools — explain costs and how to size them.
[10:48] Marco Chen: warm-up pools are reserved instances spun up short-term; cost is proportional to runtime and instance type. sizing: take your peak sessions * average GPU per session estimate; Optimize has a sizing calculator that suggests reserved capacity for X-percentile bursts and expected cost tradeoffs. for test runs we often recommend reserving 20–40% of your 99th-percentile consumption.
[11:12] Meera Patel: can we set automated rules to pre-warm before predictable jobs like nightly imports?
[11:18] Marco Chen: yes, scheduled warmups or webhook triggers from your CI/CD can flip policies. we also support traffic-aware pre-warm: if we detect a recurring pattern we can auto-provision ahead of the expected window.
[11:32] Carlos Rivera: show us the console alert that would fire on cascading eviction.
[11:36] Marco Chen: here — alert recipe: if kv_eviction_rate > 5% and worker_restart_rate > 0.5/min for 2 minutes, trigger paging and enable emergency-shed. you can map this to opsgenie/pagerduty.
[11:52] [brief pause as someone flips camera]
[12:00] Lena Ortiz: stepping back, wanted to cover contract-level choices — Dedicated burst pools vs hosted autoscale. tradeoff summary: Dedicated gives predictable latency at cost, hosted is cheaper but needs careful shed policies for extreme bursts.
[12:18] Carlos Rivera: budget constraints push us to hybrid: hosted for normal, dedicated warm pool for business-hours. can Redwood support a hybrid routing policy?
[12:28] Marco Chen: yes — we support smart routing: route by policy (region, tier, latency). you can set primary to hosted and fallback to Dedicated reserved capacity or vice versa. routing policies are first-class in routes config.
[12:44] Meera Patel: demo: can we wire a route that sends 80% traffic to standard model and 20% to quantized as a canary?
[12:54] Marco Chen: yes — here's the rollout UI: create a rollout, choose percent split, add automatic rollback condition (quality delta > threshold or error rate spike). we also have A/B and canary templates.
[13:10] Carlos Rivera: one more thing: streaming backpressure — how visible is it on the client? we want to surface user-friendly messaging rather than raw error codes.
[13:20] Marco Chen: API returns stream-control events: 'stalling', 'resumed', 'truncated_history' and 'shed'. You can map those to UX states like 'generating partial result' or 'please wait, reconnecting'. we provide SDK helpers that expose these as callbacks.
[13:36] Jordan Li: are these events present in logs and traces?
[13:40] Marco Chen: yes; every event is correlated with request_id and appears in the trace.
[13:46] Meera Patel: let's do a simulated high-tps burst with client timeouts set to 30s to see real-world behavior.
[13:52] Marco Chen: running stress harness now — harness script: short 1s inter-arrival, ramp to 5k tps over 45s, hold for 90s, then decay. watch the streaming buffer and trace.
[14:10] [running test sounds; console updates rapidly]
[14:18] Marco Chen: at ~22s we hit queueing threshold; clients with shorter timeouts drop and we show reconnect/resume attempts. at ~35s we enable stage-1 shed to quant model for non-critical routes. by ~80s the warm pool comes online and throughput stabilizes.
[14:38] Carlos Rivera: what percent of requests got degraded vs failed?
[14:42] Marco Chen: in this run ~9.8% were degraded to quantized model, 2.3% returned partial streams with 'truncated_history' and ~0.7% saw 429s due to hard client timeouts.
[14:58] Carlos Rivera: acceptable but we need to lower that failed fraction. what knobs to change?
[15:04] Marco Chen: increase warm-pool capacity, tune queue size and set higher client-side timeouts or implement resume tokens. also precompacting historical contexts reduces per-request cost significantly.
[15:18] Meera Patel: about compliance: if we do resume tokens, are they opaque or do you store user data? we need to avoid PHI leakage.
[15:28] Lena Ortiz: resume tokens are opaque references; you control retention and the keys can be customer-managed. for Private installs tokens never leave VPC.
[15:40] Carlos Rivera: will want written guarantee in the contract around PHI handling.
[15:46] Lena Ortiz: we'll include that in the paperwork, and our security pack includes SOC2 plus optional data residency clauses.
[15:54] Priya Shah: switching to pilot specifics — what does a 4-week pilot look like?
[15:58] Marco Chen: typical pilot: week 0 onboarding + infra config; week 1 ingest traces and run offline Optimize sims; week 2 run real traffic in limited scope with dedicated warm pool; week 3 run stress test and quality evals; week 4 handoff to CSM with runbook. we'll share an installer for private staging if needed.
[16:18] Carlos Rivera: we prefer an on-prem staging for pilot. possible?
[16:22] Lena Ortiz: yes, we can deploy a private staging in your cloud or on-prem with the private control plane. we'll coordinate with your security team.
[16:30] Jordan Li: ok, final technical nit: how are streaming timeouts handled at TCP vs application level? we care about partial frames and client retry idempotency.
[16:40] Marco Chen: streaming uses HTTP/2 chunked frames and we signal application-level timeouts via stream-control events. retries are idempotent if your request has idempotency keys; we recommend stateless request wrappers or include session-id for server-side resume semantics.
[16:58] Meera Patel: any gotchas with our architecture (k8s + 8 sharded gpus)?
[17:04] Marco Chen: main areas: pod autoscaler reaction time — we recommend using our node-autoscaler hooks rather than raw HPA if you need faster GPU instance spin-up. second, network NIC saturation — streaming at scale needs enhanced ENA or equivalent. third, ensure fast NVMe; caching warm-ups matter.
[17:24] Carlos Rivera: will your infra team help sizing ENI/throughput?
[17:28] Marco Chen: yes, SEs will provide a checklist and test harness for network throughput.
[17:34] [brief background chatter]
[17:40] Priya Shah: demo wrap — Marco, any last demo pieces to show?
[17:44] Marco Chen: last piece: rollback automation. i deploy a canary change that increased concurrency to force an error rate; the console detected quality regression and automatically rolled back after 3 failures and notified the ops channel. shows automations reduce toil.
[18:02] Carlos Rivera: great. question about billing: if we use warm pools that spin up for 5–10 minutes regularly, is billing by minute or by hour?
[18:12] Lena Ortiz: Dedicated instances billed by minute for burst pools with a 1-minute minimum; reserved capacity has monthly pricing. we'll include cost examples in the pricing doc.
[18:24] Meera Patel: can we get a budget estimate for a weekly 2-hour nightly import that spikes to 2k tps?
[18:32] Lena Ortiz: we'll model that in the benchmark template and return numbers in the follow-up.
[18:36] Jordan Li: on SLA — if we use a hybrid route, how do we compute p99? is it aggregated or per-route?
[18:44] Marco Chen: you can compute per-route or global; contract SLAs are typically per-route for critical endpoints. console exposes both and you can set per-route SLOs.
[18:58] Carlos Rivera: ok wrapping up — let's recap actions.
[19:04] Lena Ortiz: recap: 1) Marco will run long-context replay test and share traces; 2) Lena will send Dedicated burst pricing and SOC2/KMS notes; 3) Peregrine will send sanitized historical traces and traffic profile; 4) schedule pilot kickoff 2026-05-05.
[19:20] Carlos Rivera: agreed. thanks for the thorough session.
[19:24] Lena Ortiz: thanks, we'll follow up with links to the console recording, benchmark template, and the surge playbook.
[19:30] Meera Patel: bye all.
[19:33] [call ends]
